In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Dipolar extracellular potentials generated by axonal projections" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by Timo van Kerkoerle (Reviewer #1); Gaute T Einevoll (Reviewer #2); and Rishikesh Narayanan (Reviewer #3), and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Andrew King as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The manuscript investigates the contribution of action potentials to the local field potential, and shows how, contrary to common wisdom, axonal arbors can generate dipolar fields. The manuscript is well written and the figures are generally clear.

Essential revisions:

The revisions requested are of two-fold nature: 1) more exploration of the generality of the effects, 2) more justification and exploration of the findings.

As mentioned in the manuscript an important factor in the contribution of action potentials is the synchronicity between neighboring axons; if there is too much jitter in the spikes coming in on neighboring axons the fields generated by them will cancel it. It would be of interest to quantify what the synchronicity needs to be on neighboring axons to be able to see a significant effect in the LFP. Alternatively, for a fixed level of coherence between the spikes, what would the generated field be for different frequencies? It can be judged from Figure 3 that even for bifurcations on the same axon, the frequency has to be high to still see an effect. It would therefore be relevant to see for a realistic level of coherence between the spikes what the generated axonal field would be for different frequencies. This can help to understand whether this phenomenon could play a role in (1) high-frequency ripples, as for example measured with ECoG (Worrell et al. Brain 2008), or even in (2) high-frequency gamma activity, as measured as dipoles within the cortex (van Kerkoerle et al. PNAS 2014), or with MEG on the scalp (e.g. Siegel et al. Neuron 2008).

This result will also make it easier to judge how to relate it to the previous literature (which part of the LFP can be attributed to dipoles generated by axonal arbors), and thereby how relevant the current manuscript is for a broader audience.

The auditory brainstem of the barn owl is a rather special case where the activation is very brief, in the order of a few milliseconds. The authors also refer to early papers in the visual cortex (Mitzdorf and Singer 1978; Mitzdorf, 1985), but these are special cases where electrical stimulation of the optic radiation was used, which also gives a dipolar field in the order of milliseconds as well. In contrast, the dipolar fields as evoked by a visual stimulus, are generally in the order of tens of milliseconds (e.g. Mitzdorf, 1985; Schroeder et al., 1991; Schroeder, Mehta and Givre, 1998; Self et al., 2013). It would be relevant to understand what part of a more common visual activation like that can be attributed to axonal fields.

The paper makes it conceivable that population axonal spikes contribute to dipoles which would be measurable in the LFP and potentially even to scalp EEG/MEG.

Can the authors extract the dipole and quadrupole moments from the fit?

Can the authors assess the uniqueness of the fit in their optimization procedure? Could there be several disparate solutions to this fitting procedure, possibly resulting in significant variability in the computed moments based on the specific fit that was employed?

An improved comparison is needed between the numerically comprehensive scheme and the simplified analytical model. It would be nice to illustrate how similar they are for a well-chosen example.

"All filtering was performed with third-order Butterworth filters […] The LFP was calculated by low-pass filtering the signal with a cut-off of 1000 Hz."

The filter used by the authors to obtain the LFP is a 3rd order Butterworth with a cut-off of 1000 Hz. The cut-off frequency is large, in comparison to most studies employing a value set at 100 Hz to 500 Hz (Buzsaki, Anastassiou and Koch, 2012; Schomberg et al., 2012; Taxidis et al., 2015). Additionally, as the order of the filter is 3, the sharpness of the filter transition from the pass band to the stop band would be shallow. This implies that frequencies beyond 1000 Hz also pass through. Additionally, in some figures, the low frequency component is arbitrarily represented at an even higher 2 kHz. EFP and LFP are alternately employed, and there is a lot of ambiguity with reference to notation and terminology. The specific choice for cutoff frequencies is of utmost importance because the authors' central claim about the contributions of (high frequency) action potentials propagating through the axon to LFPs. How dependent is the filter structure for the conclusions drawn by the authors? Would the conclusions be different if the authors employed, say a 20th order Butterworth filter with a 250 Hz cutoff?

In describing the model fit, it would be valuable to describe the most important assumptions made. Also other details of modeling need attention:

a) Location of nodes of Ranvier: In the case where there were multiple axons, were the nodes of Ranvier placed at the same spatial axis?

b) "Note that in order to avoid confounding effects, the horizontal distances between axons in Figure 1C-E are for illustration only; all collaterals were simulated to lie on a straight line." Isn't this an oversimplification that artificially boosts contributions of the transmembrane currents from different axons to the EFP? What happens if this is changed to reflect an anatomical organization where horizontal distances do exist?

c) What was the structure of the axon at the bifurcations – was the surface area larger at bifurcations? What was the location of the terminal with reference to the nearest node? What would be the impact of terminating axons with a bouton with appropriate dimensions containing all ion channels (calcium, sodium and potassium especially) they are supposed to express? How would the bouton geometry (Gydikov et al., 1984 and Gydikob and Trayanova, 1986) and ion channel densities there, along with changes in each parameter mentioned here, alter the conclusions?

d) The authors assume that the myelin sheath does not contribute to the EFPs. However, given the several channels and receptors that these glial cells express, and given the active roles they play during action potential propagation, is it reasonable to assume that they don't contribute to the EFPs? What would be the contribution of the capacitative current that is consequent to the dielectric myelin between two parallel conducting media, with a high-frequency action potential propagating across? Is there any contribution of the 1/fn scaling that is generally observed in LFPs, especially given the absence of intrinsic dendritic filtering in the analysis here (Nature Reviews Neuroscience reviews of Buzsaki et al., 2012, Einevoll et al., 2013)? Could the capacitive current (with reference to the myelinated compartments), however small, contribute to such filtering?

e) Please provide details of how the infinite axon was simulated.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the context that EFPs are important in neuroscience but their physiological basis remains debated, and that axonal contributions are typically assumed negligible in current models.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 accurately describe established knowledge about EFPs and current modeling practices in the field. These are well-supported background statements that set up the motivation for the study.

results.result: The authors demonstrate both theoretically and experimentally that axonal contributions to EFPs can be significant, particularly in terminal zones with branching and terminating axons. Models predict dipolar far fields with polarity reversal at the terminal zone center, which was confirmed in barn owl nucleus laminaris recordings.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C10 represent the core findings of the manuscript. The theoretical predictions (C7, C8) from computational models are validated by experimental recordings (C9), demonstrating that axonal terminal zones produce significant EFPs with dipolar characteristics (C10). The convergence of modeling and experimental evidence provides strong support.

results.result: Simulations of long, straight axons show characteristic triphasic extracellular action potentials that translate in time with conduction velocity. The three peaks correspond to capacitive, sodium, and potassium currents, and the transmembrane current is proportional to the second spatial derivative of membrane potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 describe well-established biophysical properties of axonal action potentials supported by both simulation data (Figure 1A) and established cable theory. The attribution of peaks to specific currents is supported by citation to Gold et al. (2006).

results.result: Axonal terminations and bifurcations produce biphasic EFP responses with opposite polarities. When combined in a single axon, both features produce biphasic responses at their respective locations on the same timescale but with opposite polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are directly supported by simulation data in Figures 1B-D. The modeling demonstrates clear mechanistic effects of axonal geometry on EFP waveform shape, showing how terminations and bifurcations each produce characteristic biphasic responses.

results.result: In axon bundles with randomized geometries, population-level EFPs show polarity reversal with monophasic negative peaks in bifurcation zones, monophasic positive peaks in termination zones, and cancellation at the terminal zone center.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by simulation data in Figure 1E showing population responses. The transition from biphasic single-fiber responses to monophasic population responses is explained mechanistically by summation of responses with temporal jitter.

results.result: Three-dimensional axon bundle simulations show that low-pass filtered EFPs exhibit dipolar spatial patterns with double-lobed amplitude distributions. The polarity reversal occurs at the middle of the terminal zone where fiber number is maximal, and the EFP amplitude follows the distribution of branchings and terminations.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 are supported by detailed 3D simulation data in Figure 2A-C. The dipolar structure and its relationship to axonal anatomy are clearly demonstrated, with the counterintuitive finding that amplitude is minimal where fiber number is maximal.

results.result: Multi-unit activity (MUA) shows ellipsoidal iso-amplitude patterns centered at the terminal zone, with amplitude proportional to local fiber number rather than showing dipolar structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by simulation data in Figure 2D-F. The qualitative difference between low-frequency and high-frequency components is clearly demonstrated, with MUA reflecting local fiber density rather than dipolar geometry.

results.result: At low frequencies (<1 kHz), bifurcation zones contribute supralinearly to dipole moments, exceeding non-bifurcating controls by factor of 20 at distances >1 mm. At high frequencies (>2.5 kHz), bifurcations do not enhance dipole moments. Maximum dipole moment occurs at ~500 Hz when spatial wavelength matches terminal zone width.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by systematic frequency analysis in Figure 3. The frequency-dependent effects are well-characterized and mechanistically explained by the relationship between spatial wavelength and terminal zone geometry. The supralinear contribution at intermediate frequencies is a key theoretical prediction.

results.result: The barn owl nucleus laminaris provides an ideal experimental system with well-characterized anatomy where EFPs are mainly due to afferent axonal activity. Two fiber bundles enter NL, bifurcate at the border, and terminate within the nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 describe established anatomical and physiological knowledge about barn owl NL, supported by multiple citations. This provides strong justification for the experimental system choice.

results.result: Click-evoked responses in barn owl NL show distinct low-frequency and high-frequency components, with the high-frequency ringing reflecting frequency tuning and phase locking of incoming axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4 and citations to previous work. These observations establish the experimental phenomena to be modeled.

results.result: Model fitting to NL recordings reveals fiber number distribution consistent with known anatomy, dipolar polarity reversal in low-frequency responses, and axonal conduction velocity of 4.0 m/s (within previously reported confidence bounds of 0.4-6 m/s).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 are supported by model fitting results in Figure 5. The inferred parameters are consistent with independent anatomical and physiological measurements, providing validation of the modeling approach. The correlation coefficient R²=0.56±0.15 indicates reasonable but not perfect model fit.

results.result: Using the analytical model, the predicted axonal contribution to the auditory brainstem response (ABR) at 2 cm distance is 3.1 µV, which is of the same order of magnitude as the experimentally reported ABR amplitude of ~10 µV.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 apply the validated model to predict far-field contributions. The prediction is within the correct order of magnitude of experimental measurements, though the calculation involves simplifying assumptions about skull anatomy. This represents a reasonable extrapolation from the validated near-field model.

results.result: Synaptic contributions to EFPs in barn owl NL are expected to be small because synaptic membrane potentials are much smaller than spike impacts, and the symmetrical arrangement of synapses on spherical NL cell bodies cannot produce dipolar fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 provide reasoning for why axonal sources dominate in this system. The arguments are based on cited physiological data and anatomical constraints. While this reasoning is sound, direct experimental verification of negligible synaptic contributions would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Axonal branchings and terminations in terminal zones deform extracellular waveforms and can produce dipolar EFP structures. Such terminal zones exist throughout the nervous system, yet their contributions to EFPs are neglected in current models.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 synthesize the theoretical mechanism with anatomical prevalence. The mechanism is supported by modeling (C26-C27) and the anatomical prevalence is supported by citations (C28-C29). The critique of current models (C30) is a reasonable inference from the findings.

results.result: Similar dipolar EFP reversals have been reported in chicken NL and mammalian MSO, but were attributed to dendritic sources. Since barn owl NL lacks bipolar dendritic morphology, similar dipolar potentials in owls and mammals likely arise from different physiological substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 compare findings across species and propose that convergent EFP patterns can arise from different cellular mechanisms. This is supported by anatomical differences (C87) and represents a reasonable inference (C88) about evolutionary convergence.

results.result: Axonal growth patterns reflect trade-offs between conduction delay and wiring cost. Directed structures optimized for temporal precision should produce stronger dipolar EFPs, with maximal dipole moments when activation spread matches projection zone size.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 connect axonal structure to function. The relationship between growth optimization and structure (C89-C91) is supported by citations. The prediction about dipolar EFPs in temporally precise systems (C92-C93) is a reasonable inference from the model, though it remains to be tested experimentally.

results.result: Axonal contributions may be relevant for EEG analysis and are particularly relevant for the auditory brainstem response (ABR), which involves highly synchronized and organized axonal structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 represent speculative extensions of the findings to other recording modalities. While the reasoning is plausible and supported by one citation (C94), these remain predictions requiring experimental validation. The ABR prediction (C95) is more concrete given the order-of-magnitude calculation (C76-C78), but still requires direct experimental confirmation.

results.result: In axon bundles, fiber number varies spatially but current sources are highly correlated due to propagating action potentials. This allows recovery of normalized fiber densities and average membrane potentials from EFP recordings when axonal sources dominate.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 describe the inverse problem solution demonstrated in Figure 5. The successful model fitting (C98) validates the theoretical framework (C96-C97) for this specific case where axonal contributions dominate.

results.result: Traditional theory predicts quadrupolar far fields for straight axons that decay faster than dipolar synaptic sources. However, previous theoretical and experimental studies have reported dipolar axonal EFP structures in various brain regions, attributed to axons based on conduction velocities.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 accurately summarize established theory and previous experimental findings. The apparent contradiction between traditional theory (C18-C20) and experimental observations (C21-C25) motivates the current study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations.
